name: Nifedipine
route_note: extended-release tablets once daily; immediate-release capsules (restricted use)

discovery.note: The prototype dihydropyridine calcium antagonist, discovered in the 1960s.

tagline: Prototype dihydropyridine for angina, hypertension and preterm labour
summary: Nifedipine is the prototype dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. Extended-release forms treat hypertension and angina; it is also used for vasospastic angina, Raynaud's phenomenon and, on the WHO list, to delay preterm labour.
mechanism: Nifedipine blocks L-type calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle, relaxing arteries, including coronary arteries, and lowering peripheral resistance.
Immediate-release forms cause a rapid fall in blood pressure with reflex sympathetic activation and tachycardia, which can precipitate ischaemia; extended-release formulations avoid these peaks.
uses: Tocolysis in preterm labour (WHO listed; off-label in many countries)

history.title: FDA approval
history.detail: Approved in the US as Procardia for angina.

history.title: Procardia XL
history.detail: A once-daily osmotic (GITS) extended-release formulation is approved.

history.title: Safety concerns
history.detail: Meta-analyses link short-acting nifedipine to increased mortality in coronary disease; sublingual use for hypertensive urgency is abandoned.

history.title: ACTION
history.detail: Long-acting nifedipine is shown to be safe in stable angina.

facts: Grapefruit juice and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors raise nifedipine levels.
The empty shell of osmotic extended-release tablets can appear in stool.
